Fermentation is a process in which tiny living organisms — most commonly yeast, bacteria, or fungi — break down sugars and other organic substances to produce energy for themselves, and as a side effect of doing so, they release byproducts like alcohol, gases, or acids.

Think of it this way: these microorganisms are "eating" sugars. When they digest those sugars, they produce waste products, just like any living thing does. Those waste products — alcohol, carbon dioxide, lactic acid, and others — are what we call the products of fermentation. Many of these products turn out to be incredibly useful to us.

All living cells need energy to survive. The primary currency of energy inside a cell is a molecule called ATP. Cells typically make ATP by burning glucose (a simple sugar) using oxygen — this is called cellular respiration, and it's the normal, efficient way to make energy.

But sometimes, oxygen is unavailable or in short supply. When that happens, certain organisms and cells switch to a backup plan: fermentation. In fermentation, the cell still breaks down glucose, but without using oxygen. The key technical point is this — in fermentation, an organic molecule (rather than oxygen) acts as the final acceptor of electrons in the chemical reaction. This is what distinguishes fermentation from regular aerobic (oxygen-using) respiration.

Fermentation is a less efficient process — it produces far less ATP per sugar molecule than full aerobic respiration. But it gets the job done when oxygen isn't available.

1. Alcoholic fermentation

This is carried out primarily by yeast. Yeast breaks down glucose and produces ethanol (alcohol) and carbon dioxide (CO₂) as its waste products.

This is the process behind:

  • Bread — yeast ferments the sugars in dough and releases CO₂, which makes the bread rise and become fluffy
  • Beer and wine — yeast ferments the sugars in grains or grapes and produces alcohol
  • Any fermented beverage involving alcohol

2. Lactic acid fermentation

This is carried out primarily by lactic acid bacteria. Instead of producing alcohol and CO₂, these bacteria convert glucose into lactic acid.

This is the process behind:

  • Yogurt — bacteria ferment the lactose (milk sugar) in milk and produce lactic acid, which thickens the milk and gives yogurt its tangy taste
  • Cheese — same bacteria at work
  • Sauerkraut and kimchi — bacteria ferment the sugars in cabbage and vegetables
  • Pickles (when made the traditional way, not with vinegar)
  • Sourdough bread — a combination of wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria

Lactic acid fermentation also happens inside your own muscles. When you exercise very hard and fast — sprinting, for instance — your muscle cells can't get enough oxygen quickly enough to keep up with the energy demand. They switch temporarily to lactic acid fermentation. The lactic acid that builds up is partly responsible for the burning sensation in your muscles during intense effort.

Beyond alcohol and lactic acid, fermentation by different organisms can produce:

  • Acetic acid — the acid in vinegar (though the conversion of alcohol to acetic acid also involves oxygen, making it a borderline case of fermentation in the strict sense)
  • Carbon dioxide — used in carbonated drinks
  • Butyric acid — produced by some gut bacteria during the fermentation of dietary fibre; it plays a role in gut health

In everyday and industrial language, "fermentation" is also used in a broader sense to describe any controlled process in which microorganisms are used to produce useful substances, even if oxygen is involved. In this sense, fermentation includes:

  • Manufacturing antibiotics like penicillin (produced by fungi)
  • Making vitamins (like B12 and riboflavin)
  • Producing biofuels like ethanol from crops
  • Creating enzymes used in food processing and medicine
  • Brewing kombucha and fermenting other health drinks

This industrial usage is less technically precise than the biochemical definition, but it's widely understood and accepted.

One of fermentation's most historically important roles is food preservation. When bacteria produce lactic acid during fermentation, the environment becomes acidic (low pH). Most harmful bacteria cannot survive in acidic conditions. This is why fermented foods like sauerkraut, kimchi, and traditional pickles stay safe to eat for a long time — the fermentation process itself kills or suppresses harmful bacteria. Before refrigerators existed, fermentation was one of humanity's primary tools for keeping food safe.

It's worth being clear about what fermentation is not, to avoid confusion:

  • It is not rotting or spoiling. Rotting is uncontrolled breakdown by a random mix of organisms. Fermentation is a specific, controlled process by particular organisms.
  • It is not the same as digestion in the human stomach. However, fermentation does happen in your large intestine (colon), where gut bacteria ferment dietary fibre that your own digestive enzymes couldn't break down. This produces short-chain fatty acids and gases — which is why eating a lot of fibre can cause gas.
  • It is not always anaerobic in industrial practice, though in its strict biological definition it is.

Fermentation is the process by which microorganisms (or cells) break down sugars without oxygen to produce energy for themselves, releasing useful byproducts — alcohol, carbon dioxide, acids — that humans have used for thousands of years to make food, drinks, medicines, and fuels.
